title: What is constructive alignment?
description: Constructive alignment designs teaching and assessment to match intended learning outcomes. Biggs's model, how Australian universities use it and an example.
shortAnswer: The principle of constructive alignment is a course design approach in which the intended learning outcomes are defined first, and teaching activities and assessment tasks are then designed so that each directly supports and tests those outcomes. Developed by John Biggs, it combines the constructivist view that learners build knowledge through what they do with an aligned design, so every activity and assessment has a clear purpose.
keyTakeaways: Constructive alignment has three linked parts: intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment tasks.
The design order matters: outcomes first, assessment second, activities third.
John Biggs described the approach in Higher Education in 1996; it is widely used in Australian university teaching guidance.
Misalignment shows up as outcomes nobody assesses, or assessments that test something no outcome asks for.

sections.heading: Where does constructive alignment come from?

blocks.text: Constructive alignment comes from John Biggs, who set it out in the paper "Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment" in Higher Education, volume 32, 1996, pages 347 to 364 ([ERIC record](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ534311)). The ERIC abstract describes it as an approach to instructional design that incorporates the principles of constructivism, and presents it as generalisable to most units or programs in higher education.

The word constructive refers to the idea that learners construct meaning through their own activity. The University of Wollongong's [learning and teaching guidance](https://ltc.uow.edu.au/hub/article/constructive-alignment) quotes Biggs that "knowledge is constructed by the activities of the learner" rather than transmitted from teacher to learner. The word alignment refers to designing teaching and assessment to fit the intended outcomes.

sections.heading: How does constructive alignment work in course design?

blocks.text: Constructive alignment works by designing in a fixed order: define the [learning outcomes](/glossary/learning-outcomes), design assessment tasks that require learners to demonstrate them, then choose teaching activities that prepare learners for those tasks.

blocks.caption: The three components of constructive alignment
head: Component
Design question
Common failure
rows: What should learners be able to do at the end?
Outcomes written as topics, or with verbs that cannot be observed
What evidence would show each outcome is achieved?
Tasks test recall when the outcome asks for application
What must learners do to be ready for the assessment?
Activities are delivered because they always have been, not because an outcome needs them

blocks.text: The UNSW [guidance on aligning assessment with outcomes](https://www.teaching.unsw.edu.au/aligning-assessment-learning-outcomes) advises making sure "that every learning outcome is assessed, and that every assessment maps onto a learning outcome", and notes that mapping outcomes to activities and tasks in a table can reveal outcomes that are ignored or activities unrelated to any outcome.

sections.heading: How does constructive alignment relate to Australian standards?

blocks.text: The Higher Education Standards Framework does not name constructive alignment, but it requires the same result. Standard 1.4.3 of the [Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards) 2021](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2021L00488/latest/text) requires that "Methods of assessment are consistent with the learning outcomes being assessed", and Standard 3.1.3 requires teaching and learning activities that foster "progressive and coherent achievement of expected learning outcomes".

The Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) [course design guidance note](https://www.teqsa.gov.au/guides-resources/resources/guidance-notes/guidance-note-course-design-including-learning-outcomes-and-assessment) warns that if achievement and assessment of outcomes are not aligned, outcomes may not be achieved or adequately assessed. In VET, a similar logic applies through units of competency, where assessment must be consistent with the training product.

sections.heading: How is constructive alignment different from curriculum mapping?

blocks.text: Constructive alignment is the design principle; [curriculum mapping](/glossary/curriculum-mapping) is a method for checking and documenting alignment across a whole program. An [assessment blueprint](/glossary/assessment-blueprint) applies the same idea at the level of a single assessment, specifying which outcomes each item or task covers.

sections.heading: What does an aligned design look like?

blocks.text: Illustrative example: a workplace course on handling customer complaints in a regulated financial firm.

head: Outcome
Assessment
Activity
rows: Classify a customer contact as a complaint under the firm's policy
Classify ten recorded contacts; eight or more correct
Guided practice classifying sample contacts, with feedback
Respond to a complaint within the required steps and timeframes
Role play marked against a checklist
Worked demonstration, then paired role plays
Case discussion of past systemic issues

blocks.text: A slide based lecture on complaint handling history would be cut: it supports no outcome and no assessment.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry applies alignment structurally: each outcome in the framework must have an assessment point before content is generated, and content is traced to the outcomes it serves. Orphan content and unassessed outcomes show up as gaps.

faqs.q: Is constructive alignment only for universities?
faqs.a: No. Biggs developed it for higher education, but the principle applies to any structured learning, including workplace compliance and VET programs. Any program that defines outcomes and assesses them benefits from checking that teaching and assessment actually match those outcomes.

faqs.q: What is the difference between alignment and teaching to the test?
faqs.a: Teaching to the test narrows learning to whatever the assessment happens to check. Constructive alignment starts from the outcomes and designs the assessment to require them, so preparing for the assessment means achieving the outcomes. If the assessment is well designed, the two converge; if not, alignment exposes the problem.

faqs.q: Which book explains constructive alignment in detail?
faqs.a: Biggs and Catherine Tang's book Teaching for Quality Learning at University is the standard extended treatment. It is listed in the University of Wollongong's constructive alignment guidance, and UNSW's guidance on aligning assessment with outcomes also draws on Biggs and Tang, including their SOLO taxonomy.
